name: The unresolved problem of social order: Rome versus the City of God
plain_explanation: Ancient civilization ended its chaos through the Roman Empire -- an actual, workable state, but merely a brute fact with no ennobling idea behind it. Medieval civilization proposed the Church as an ideal of universal order, but this idea was never fully realized in practice. Russell argues the modern world is drifting back toward a Rome-like solution (order imposed by force) and that a truly durable order needs both the practical solidity of Rome and the moral idealism of Augustine's City of God.
precise_definition: Russell's closing diagnosis: 'The ancient world found an end to anarchy in the Roman Empire, but the Roman Empire was a brute fact, not an idea. The Catholic world sought an end to anarchy in the Church, which was an idea, but was never adequately embodied in fact... The problem of a durable and satisfactory social order can only be solved by combining the solidity of the Roman Empire with the idealism of Saint Augustine's City of God.'
why_it_mattered: This is the chapter's final thesis and effectively states the normative problem that Russell implies the rest of modern philosophy -- and his own book -- must try to address.
historical_origin: Draws on Russell's earlier treatment of the Roman Empire (Book One) and of Augustine's City of God (Book Two).
competing_positions: A social order 'imposed by force, representing the will of the powerful rather than the hopes of common men' -- the direction Russell says the modern world seemed, in 1945, to be moving toward
influence_on_later_thinkers: Frames the entire remainder of the History as, implicitly, a search for the 'new philosophy' Russell says will be needed.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Explicitly political and religious: contrasts the Roman state with the Christian ideal of the City of God.
